The cloak is cylindrical with inner radius a = 3 cm and outer radius b = 9 cm.
The background medium is designed with permittivity ε = 10^-3 and permeability μ = 10^7 to match free space parameters.
The cloak shell consists of 15 concentric layers of L-C metamaterial unit cells, each layer divided into 90 angular segments (4° span).
The unit cell consists of two series inductors and one shunt capacitor mounted on an FR-4 substrate of 1 mm thickness.
The design frequency is 40 MHz, with the excitation pulse cutoff frequency approximately 40 MHz.
The excitation pulse is a Blackmann-Harris pulse lasting 90 ns.
The vector network analyzer (VNA) measures transmission scattering parameters to extract time-domain responses.
The experimental device measures about 400 mm × 400 mm × 1 mm.
The cloak reduces scattered energy by more than a factor of 10 compared to a bare metallic cylinder.
Time delay of about 73 ns is observed between points inside and outside the cloak, consistent with simulation.
Pulse broadening and time delay effects are minimal due to low dispersion from the nonresonant L-C network.
The cloak parameters are anisotropic and spatially inhomogeneous, diagonalized in cylindrical coordinates.
The cloak device is rotationally symmetric.
Bloch impedances are used at the outer boundary to mimic an infinite background and reduce reflections.
The scattered energy distribution with the cloak is nearly isotropic over all angles.
The experimental results closely match numerical simulations of the cloak behavior.
The cloak is designed based on transformation optics principles applied to L-C transmission line networks.
The nonuniform L-C network independently tunes permittivity and permeability tensor components.
The cloak is effective for broadband electromagnetic pulses, not just monochromatic waves.
The study experimentally verifies dynamic pulse propagation effects through the cloak, including time evolution of the pulse.
